question: Almost six years after the deadline for implementation, six Member States have still not fulfilled the EU requirements laid down in the European Electronic Communications Code1 (EECC) to roll out technologies to improve safety during emergencies. Article 109 EECC required Member States to implement advanced caller location by December 2020. Poland, Cyprus and Malta have not yet done so.

Article 110 EECC required Member States to implement a mobile-based public warning system by June 2022. Ireland, Slovakia and Finland have yet to implement such a system. Both technologies play a critical role in improving public safety by helping emergency services quickly locate people in need and by allowing civil protection authorities to send warnings to people about imminent threats. 1.
Does the Commission agree that advanced caller location and mobile-based public warning systems improve public safety and societal resilience?

Will the Commission initiate proceedings against the Member States that have not fulfilled their obligations under Articles 109 and 110 EECC, or in the future, Articles 106 and 107 of the proposed digital networks act?
If not, how can the Commission ensure that its future laws on preparedness will be implemented effectively if Member States face no consequences for non-compliance?

Directive (EU) 2018/1972 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 December 2018 establishing the European Electronic Communications Code (Recast) (OJ L 321, 17.12.2018, p. 36, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2018/1972/oj). 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.9.2026) Caller location information, which applies to all emergency communications, improves the level of protection and the security of end-users and assists the emergency services in the discharge of their duties.

In that context, the Commission is continuously monitoring the implementation of the European Electronic Communications Code (Directive 2018/19721, ‘EECC’) as presented in the 2024 Report on the implementation of the EU emergency number 1122. The next report will be published by the end of 2026.

On the basis of the data received, the Commission will assess the state of implementation of effective emergency communication in the EU and, where the data will indicate shortcomings in implementation, will consider appropriate follow-up, including enforcement action where relevant.

The Commission also monitors the implementation of public warning systems that have been identified as an important element in the Preparedness Union Strategy and in the Ninistö report. The Commission is currently reviewing the provisions of the EECC, including those aimed to ensure access to emergency communications, and public warning systems provided through electronic communication services.
In this context, the Commission monitors the implementation of the relevant legal provisions, including Articles 109 and 110 of the EECC, by Member States and may dedide to take appropriate action.

In addition, and beyond the EECC requirements, the Commission works towards the delivery of the Galileo Emergency Warning Satellite Service that offers a complementary means of disseminating public warning messages in case of emergencies.
